Like in Romanian! Before e, i: "ch", "j" sounds (cena, città, gelato, Giulia). Before a, o, u: hard "k" and "g" (casa, gatto).
Also like in Romanian: "che", "chi", "ghe", "ghi" = hard k and g. Chiavi = "kyavi", spaghetti = "spaghetti".
GN = a soft "ny", said smoothly, without the "g": signora = "si-nyo-ra", gnocchi = "nyokki". GLI = a very soft "ly", with the tongue against the roof of the mouth: famiglia = "fa-mi-lya".
SC before e, i = "sh": "scena" = "shena". Before a, o, u = "sk": scusi = "skuzi", scuola.
A double consonant is held longer, with a tiny pause: nonno (grandfather) ≠ nono (ninth), notte, mille, bello. If you say it single, the meaning can change!
The stress usually falls on the second-to-last syllable: buon-GIOR-no, ar-ri-ve-DER-ci. When it falls on the last, it's written: città, è, perché.
1. How to greet: ciao, buongiorno, buonasera
Italians greet a lot and warmly. Your choice depends on the time of day and how well you know the person.
in the morning and until the afternoon
only at bedtime / when leaving at night
with friends, family, children (also when leaving)
neutral, when you're not sure whether to use "tu" or "Lei"
"Ciao" is only for people you address with "tu". To an official, an older shop assistant or a lady you don't know, say "buongiorno" or "buonasera".
Have a nice day! (very common when parting)
2. Pronouns and the good news: you can leave them out

Just as in Romanian, in Italian the pronoun is usually NOT said, because the verb ending shows the person: "Sono Matei" = "I'm Matei". You say it only for emphasis: "Io sono di Firenze" = "I am from Florence".

The polite form is "Lei" (she), often capitalised, and the verb is in the third person: "Lei è italiano?" = "Are you Italian?", literally "Is she Italian?". It feels odd at first, but you get used to it quickly. Graziella and Matei don't know each other, so they use "Lei".
ESSERE is the most important verb. It looks a lot like Romanian "a fi": "sono" = "sunt", "siamo" = "suntem".
Watch the accent: "è" (with accent) = is; "e" (without) = and. "Matei è rumeno e Graziella è italiana."
2) The city you're from: I'm from Sibiu.
"Come stai?" (how are you?) uses the verb STARE, not ESSERE: "Come stai? — Sto bene, grazie." With "Lei": "Come sta?".
4. Nationality and job: no article, masculine and feminine
As in Romanian, after "essere" the job and nationality have NO article: "Sono restauratore", not "Sono un restauratore".
Many adjectives end in -o in the masculine and -a in the feminine; others end in -e and are the same for both:
Nationalities are written in lower case: "sono rumeno". The country is capitalised: "la Romania", "l'Italia".
5. Negation: NON, as simple as in Romanian
Italian is very easy for Romanians here: you put "non" before the verb, exactly as you put "nu".
In an answer, say "no" and then the sentence with "non": "No, non sono studente." = "No, I'm not a student."
In Italian, a yes/no question has the same word order as the statement. Only the intonation changes, rising at the end, as in Romanian.
"Vero?" at the end = "isn't it? / aren't you?": "Lei non è italiano, vero?"
What do you say at 7 pm when you walk into the trattoria?
In the evening: "buonasera". "Buonanotte" only at bedtime.
